list.listitem: Consider West Nile virus (WNV) in patients with unexplained febrile illness, meningitis and/or encephalitis, or flaccid paralysis during mosquito season. C
The majority of patients infected with WNV will remain asymptomatic (80%), however approximately 20% will develop West Nile fever, a self-limited mild febrile illness.C

Although neuroinvasive disease is a rare manifestation of WNV infection, occurring in less than 1% of infected patients, it nevertheless comprises a large portion of the morbidity and mortality associated with WNV.C
One in 150 develop severe disease; age older than 75 years and diabetes are each independent risk factors for death. C

Serum testing for virus-specific immunoglobulin M (IgM) is the easiest and most sensitive test for WNV, and a positive test in a patient with a compatible clinical presentation has a high predictive value for the diagnosis of WNV. C
Care is generally supportive, although controlled studies to evaluate pharmacologic treatment are under way. C

background.definition: West Nile virus (WNV) is a predominantly mosquito-borne flavivirus that produces a spectrum of disease in humans ranging from asymptomatic to fulminant meningitis and encephalitis.

list.listitem: A total of 2,647 cases of WNV infection reported to the CDC in 2018, 1,658 of which produced meningitis or encephalitis.
More than 21,000 cases of neuroinvasive disease in patients with WNV infection have been reported in the USA between 1999 and 2016, of which almost 1,900 resulted in death.
During a recent US outbreak, 79% of infected patients missed school or work for a median of 10 days, and 30% required hospitalization.
Nearly all human cases are due to mosquito bites.

There is rare but documented spread through blood transfusion, organ transplantation (4 cases), breast milk (1 case), occupational exposure (2 cases involving laboratory workers), and the transplacental route.
The peak incidence in the United States is in late summer and early fall, although there are sporadic year-round cases in the southern United States.
A study found that about 1 in 8000 blood transfusions were positive for WNV during a seasonal outbreak in New York City.
Infected adult mosquitoes transmit the virus to humans.

Wild birds develop high levels of viremia and serve as amplifying hosts but remain generally asymptomatic, although recent US outbreaks have been preceded by unusually high death rates of infected birds.
The incubation period ranges from 2 to 14 days but is sometimes longer in the immunocompromised.
The virus is believed to infect fibroblasts, endothelial cells, or the reticuloendothelial system.
Lower motor neuron dysfunction is believed to be due to anterior horn cell involvement and/or motor axonal neuropathy.
Use mosquito repellent when outdoors, especially between dusk and dawn. C
DEET-containing repellents provide longer periods of protection than non-DEET repellents. B
A human vaccine for WNV is in Phase 2 clinical trial.C
Eradicate stagnant waters, which serve as mosquito breeding grounds. C
Avoid mosquito bites with EPA-registered insect repellents.
Eradicate stagnant waters, which serve as mosquito breeding grounds.
While most patients are asymptomatic, 1 in 5 develops West Nile fever, a self-limited mild febrile illness. C

Consider WNV in febrile patients in endemic areas in late spring through early fall with unexplained neurologic symptoms including mental status change, muscle weakness, flaccid paralysis, and headache. C
WNV-specific IgM assay by antibody capture enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (MAC-ELISA) of serum or CSF 8 to 21 days after symptom onset is the most sensitive laboratory test. C
Serum leukocyte counts are usually normal or mildly elevated. C
The CSF usually demonstrates an elevated protein level, a lymphocytic-predominant pleocytosis, and normal glucose. C

Diagnostic criteria for confirmation of neuroinvasive WNV in symptomatic patients include 1 (4x increase in serum WNV IgM or IgG in samples taken 10-28 days apart OR 2) CSF positive for WNV IgM by PCR. C.

list.listitem: Prominent features of WNV infection include fever, headache, and altered mental status, although clinical features may vary between outbreaks ().

A systematic review of studies of patients with neuroinvasive disease found that the most common symptoms are fever (88%), nausea or vomiting (58%), fatigue (50%), headache (50%), altered mental status (39%) and focal weakness (32%).
While headache is a prominent feature of WNV infection, it is not necessarily an indicator of neuroinvasive disease.
Profound muscle weakness (flaccid paralysis) was a common complication of the encephalopathic patients of the 1999 New York City epidemic.
WNV-associated poliomyelitis presents as an acute onset of asymmetric weakness or paralysis without sensory deficit.
A maculopapular rash involving the chest, back, and arms was noted in the 2003 Colorado and 2002 Canadian outbreaks.
Movement disorders, including tremor, myoclonus, and Parkinson-like features, were noted during the 2002 Louisiana outbreak.
Ocular manifestations include chorioretinitis, iridocyclitis, and uveitis. In a study, multifocal chorioretinitis was documented in 75% of WNV-infected patients.
The initial tests of choice are serum IgM and immunoglobulin G (IgG.) See for diagnostic criteria and for interpretation.

Serum IgM (ELISA) has a 90% sensitivity and a greater than 90% specificity within 8 to 14 days of symptom onset. Since IgM does not cross an intact blood-brain barrier, a single positive IgM titer in the CSF is diagnostic of CNS infection.

A new FDA-approved lateral-flow diagnostic screening test (RapidWN) WNV IgM ELISA demonstrated a 98.8% sensitivity (range: 96.0%-100%), 95.3% specificity (range: 90.9%-100%), positive predictive value of 96.3% (range: 94.7%-100%), and a negative predictive value of 98.4% (range: 95.5%-100%).

IgM antibody may last for longer than a year; thus the presence of IgM may be unrelated to the current illness. Antibodies to other flaviviruses may cross-react; use of the plaque reduction neutralization test may help in differentiation, although some degree of cross-reactivity still exists. Recent vaccination to related flaviviruses (yellow fever, dengue) may produce false-positive ELISA results.
Serum WBCs are typically normal or mildly elevated.
CSF studies demonstrate an elevated protein level, lymphocytic-predominant pleocytosis, a normal glucose, and negative Gram stain and bacterial cultures.
CT typically demonstrates no disease-specific findings, although it may be helpful in ruling out other pathologies. MRI may show leptomeningeal or parenchymal changes.
Hyponatremia was noted in 42% of cases in a 2000 US outbreak.
The utility of polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is limited due to the transient and short-lived viremic period in humans. However, PCR assays are under development and looks promising.
Viral culture is the diagnostic gold standard, but its clinical use is limited and rarely positive except in autopsy specimens.
Abnormal EEG findings, most notably anterior predominant EEG changes, are seen in neuroinvasive disease.
No relevant clinical decision rules are found.
WNV infection should be suspected in patients with fever, headache, and altered mental status.
Initial testing should include serum IgM and IgG; see for official laboratory criteria for diagnosis and for interpretation.
Viral culture, CT, and PCR are of limited value.
Treatment of WNR infection is supportive. C
Consider acyclovir until HSV encephalitis can be excluded. C
A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled study using alpha-interferon for neuroinvasive WNV is ongoing. C

Treatment is supportive, including IV hydration for volume depletion secondary to nausea and vomiting, pain control for headache associated with meningitis, and mechanical ventilation for those with flaccid paralysis or profound encephalopathy.
Consider acyclovir treatment until HSV encephalitis is excluded.

In vitro studies have suggested that interferon alfa-2b may be a useful treatment for WNV infection, and a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trial to evaluate interferon alfa is ongoing.
A study exploring the safety and efficacy of AVI-4020 injection for WNV infection is ongoing.
A meta-analysis of largely observational trials did not support the efficacy of steroids for viral encephalitis including WNV.
A single small and underpowered trial did not find a benefit from intravenous immunoglobulin for patients with neuroinvasive WNV.
Hospitalize patients with suspected WNV infection for management of complications including dehydration, respiratory failure, seizures, and cerebral edema.
West Nile fever is a self-limited illness that resolves in 3 to 6 days. C
Patients at greatest risk for neuroinvasive disease and death are the young, the elderly, and the immunocompromised C
The incidence of encephalitis and death increases 20-fold in persons older than 50 years. C
Among patients with neuroinvasive disease, mortality is 9.2% and increases to 42% among those requiring ICU admission.

In a 1.5-year follow-up study of 54 individuals recovering from the WNV disease syndromes of fever, meningitis, or encephalitis, persistent symptoms, diminished quality of life, and functional impairment were reported by 50% of patients who had fever and 75% each of patients with either meningitis or encephalitis. Although most had normal cognitive function and returned to independent living despite persistent subjective complaints, a minority displayed subtle neurocognitive deficits on cognitive testing more than 18 months following acute disease.

In a Canadian follow-up study of 156 persons, 7 died shortly after diagnosis but the remaining patients, including those with neuroinvasive disease, had complete recovery at 1 year based on self-report measures.

A systematic review identified descriptions of over 45,000 cases, but noted significant problems with the existing literature including a high degree of heterogeneity, reliance on self-report, and a failure to compare outcomes with uninfected controls. The most common symptoms were muscle weakness, memory loss, and impairment of activities of daily living; older men with cardiovascular disease or cancer were more susceptible to long-term sequelae.

A prospective study of 55 patients across North America found that the development of acute flaccid paralysis is a predictor of mortality, and that 5 of 7 patients who died had initially presented in a coma.
Recommend use of a DEET-containing mosquito repellent when outdoors, especially between dusk and dawn.
Eradicate areas of standing water that can serve as mosquito breeding grounds.
Age older than 75 years is an independent risk for death.
Patients with transplanted organs are at greater risk of severe neuroinvasive disease; education and transmission prevention may be of greater importance in this population.
There is no defined relationship between WNV infection and fetal abnormalities.
In a study of 549 infants following a community epidemic, there were no significant differences in birth outcomes among seropositive and seronegative mothers.
Transmission of WNV through breast milk is thought to be rare, but more information is needed.
Enroll patients with suspected WNV infection during pregnancy in a CDC registry by calling 970-221-6400.
Screening of asymptomatic pregnant women for WNV is not recommended.
If WNV is diagnosed during pregnancy, consider a detailed fetal ultrasound for structural abnormalities no sooner than 2 to 4 weeks after onset of maternal WNV illness.

Examine infants born to a mother with known or suspected WNV infection during the pregnancy with attention to neurologic abnormalities, dysmorphic features, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and skin lesions and rashes.
Test infant serum for WNV-specific IgM and IgG within 2 days of birth and at 8 weeks of age.
Perform a newborn hearing screen within 1 month of birth.
Have a pathologist examine the placenta. Preserve the placenta, a sample of umbilical cord tissue, and an umbilical cord serum sample for further studies if necessary.

feature.feature_body: Fourfold or greater change in virus-specific serum antibody titer, OR Isolation of virus from or demonstration of specific viral antigen or genomic sequences in tissue, blood, CSF, or other body fluid, OR Virus-specific immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies demonstrated in CSF by antibody-capture enzyme immunoassay (EIA), OR Virus-specific IgM antibodies demonstrated in serum by antibody-capture EIA and confirmed by demonstration of virus-specific serum immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies in the same or a later specimen by another serologic assay (eg, neutralization or hemagglutination inhibition). From Encephalitis or Meningitis, Arboviral (includes California serogroup, Eastern equine, St. Louis, Western equine, West Nile, Powassan). Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2001.
